outline.chapter_title: Chapter 1 – Factual Synopsis and Procedural Posture
outline.description: This chapter presents the factual matrix underlying the government’s “pump‑and‑dump” allegations, identifies the defendants and their alleged profits, explains the statutory charges filed, and traces the procedural journey from the superseding indictment through the district court’s dismissal to the Fifth Circuit appeal.
subtopics: The alleged "pump‑and‑dump" scheme executed via social‑media platforms
Defendants’ roles, follower bases, and purported $114 million profit
Statutory counts charged – conspiracy under 18 U.S.C. §1349 and securities fraud under §§1348 & 2
Key provisions of the superseding indictment (¶¶ 13–14)
District court’s dismissal rationale – alleged failure to allege deprivation of a traditional property interest
Timeliness and scope of the government’s appeal

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 2 – Governing Law: Securities Fraud Statutes and Fraud Theories
outline.description: This chapter outlines the statutory framework that criminalizes securities fraud, explains how it borrows concepts from mail‑ and wire‑fraud law, differentiates the fraudulent‑inducement theory from the rejected right‑to‑control theory, and reviews Supreme Court precedents that shape those doctrines.
subtopics: "Scheme to defraud" and "intent to defraud" elements in 18 U.S.C. §1348
Relationship between securities fraud provisions and mail/wire fraud statutes
Definition and scope of fraudulent‑inducement theory
Definition and limitations of right‑to‑control theory
Ciminelli v. United States (2023) – why deprivation of valuable information alone is insufficient
Kousisis v. United States (2025) – affirmation that a victim need not suffer an economic loss when money or property is obtained
How these theories interact with traditional property‑interest analysis in fraud cases

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 3 – Standard for Indictment Sufficiency in the Fifth Circuit
outline.description: This chapter explains the de novo standard applied by the Fifth Circuit when reviewing whether an indictment contains all elements required by law, detailing the three statutory requirements for a sufficient indictment and citing controlling appellate authority.
subtopics: "De novo" review principle – United States v. Rafoi (2023)
Indictment must enumerate each prima facie element
"Fair notice" requirement for defendants
"Double jeopardy" safeguard against subsequent prosecution
Key precedents clarifying sufficiency standards: United States v. Fontenot (2011), United States v. Gaytan (1996), United States v. Guzman‑Ocampo (2000)
Practical implications for prosecutors drafting fraud indictments

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 4 – The Fifth Circuit’s Reasoning in Constantinescu
outline.description: This chapter dissects the court’s analysis applied to each contested element—scheme to defraud and intent to defraud—showing how it distinguished the case from Ciminelli, embraced Kousisis’ fraudulent‑inducement framework, and concluded that the indictment adequately alleged both elements.
subtopics: "Scheme to defraud" analysis – material misrepresentations about securities on social media
"Induced purchase" as deprivation of victims’ money/property
"Intent to defraud" analysis – profit motive evidence in ¶ 13‒14 versus requirement for victim harm
Rejection of district court’s reliance on a property‑interest argument
Application of Kousisis: violations exist even when defendant provides equal value or no net loss occurs
Distinguishing facts from Ciminelli’s right‑to‑control scenario
Supporting authority affirming that deception aimed at obtaining money/property satisfies both statutory elements

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 5 – Holding, Remand, and Broader Significance
